phase3_findings.description: No test covers handing the conversation turn to a queued waiter after the holding call is cancelled. Every cancellation test in tests/unit/test_query_database_queue.py either cancels a call with no waiter parked behind it or cancels the waiter instead of the holder, so the entry.lock.release() in _conversation_turn's finally block is never exercised with someone waiting on it. A regression that dropped or moved that release would leave the next call on the same conversation id blocked until its client times out while the suite still passes, because the entry's user count still reaches zero and the registry-empty assertions still hold.

The cancel-rollback seam is reached by getattr(store, "truncate_messages", None) instead of being declared on a type. The ConversationStore abstract base class in src/sqllens/agent/core/storage/base.py does not declare the method, so the caller carries two defensive log-only arms for a method the shipped BoundedConversationStore always provides, and swapping in another store would lose the rollback with only a log line. Both _conversation_baseline and _rollback_conversation also take agent: Any, so nothing checks the attributes they read.

The docstring of stream_request still says "Yields text chunks as they arrive", but after this change the whole stream is drained on a worker thread and every chunk is yielded only after get_final_message() returns. The inline comment a few lines below states the new behaviour correctly, so the two contradict each other. The 4.1.5 behavior-inert prose cap covers this finding at Suggestion, which keeps it out of the self-contradicting-diff carve-out.

BoundedConversationStore.truncate_messages returns the same False for an unknown or evicted conversation id, a user-id mismatch, and a conversation already at or below the requested length. The caller logs all three with one INFO line saying there was nothing to roll back, at src/sqllens/tools/query_database.py lines 277 to 285. In the mismatch case the conversation still carries the cancelled call's messages, so the state is not fine and the log says it is. With the shipped static user resolver the user id is constant, so this case cannot be reached under the default wiring.

The docstring of truncate_messages describes the True and False outcomes in detail but never mentions that the method raises ValueError for a negative length. The new test test_truncate_messages_rejects_a_negative_length pins behaviour the docstring does not describe.

_ConversationQueueEntry is a record with no behaviour whose invariant is maintained by two free functions. The increment lives in _conversation_turn and the matching decrement in _release_queue_entry, and the "registered exactly while users is above zero" half is only reachable through a module-level global the entry knows nothing about. A future call site that takes entry.lock directly, or that misses one of the release calls on an error path, would break the no-overlap guarantee with no signal, and users: int = 0 admits a negative count that the <= 0 test then tolerates silently.

truncate_messages takes a bare user_id: str while every sibling method takes a User and compares conversation.user.id. The result is a signature whose first two arguments are both unconstrained strings with different meanings, so swapping them still type-checks and returns the same False that the legitimate evicted-conversation case returns.

The comment bodies spend most of their length on how the design was derived and on why a branch is unreachable under the default wiring, and the same reasoning is restated a third time inside the except Exception body. The load-bearing instructions are already stated in the first sentences.

Propagation of the profile row cap through the ContextVar is pinned for the Postgres runner only, by test_profile_row_cap_reaches_offloaded_runner. Criterion nine is runner-agnostic and the MySQL and SQLite runners each received their own offload hop in this change, so switching either of them to loop.run_in_executor would silently widen that runner's fetch back to the base max_rows with no test failing.

test_second_call_starts_after_first_fails never starts a second call. Its docstring says a failed first call releases the turn like a returning one, but the body runs one failing call and asserts only that the queue registry is empty, so the named behaviour is not executed.

The shutdown explanation attributes uvicorn's use of asyncio.run and asyncio.Runner to uvicorn/_compat.py, and one agent could not confirm that file path because uvicorn was not readable from its view. Three other agents reported confirming the same path against the installed uvicorn 0.54.0, and the surrounding behavioural claim about shutdown waiting for executor threads matches CPython, so this is recorded as unverified rather than false. Checklist item VC-23 is INCONCLUSIVE for the same reason.

acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] While a `query_database` call is blocked inside a synchronous Anthropic client call or inside a synchronous database driver call (connect, execute or fetch), the event loop keeps running other tasks, and the HTTP transport answers `GET /healthz`. This holds for non-streaming and streaming Anthropic requests and for each of the Postgres, MySQL and SQLite runners.
- [ ] Two `query_database` calls with different conversation ids, each blocked inside a synchronous Anthropic or database call, are blocked at the same time: neither waits for the other call to finish before entering its own blocking call.
- [ ] Two `query_database` calls with the same conversation id do not overlap: the second call's agent run starts only after the first call has returned, failed or been cancelled. When both calls return or fail, the conversation's history afterwards holds the first call's messages followed by the second call's messages.
- [ ] After every call on a conversation has returned, failed or been cancelled — including a call cancelled while it was waiting for its turn — the server holds no per-conversation queue entry for that conversation id.
- [ ] When a `query_database` call is cancelled while it is running, the conversation holds none of the messages that call added and keeps every message that was in it when the cancelled call's turn began (after any earlier call on that conversation id finished). The next call on that conversation id runs with that history.
- [ ] When a `query_database` call is cancelled, the tool function raises the cancellation and returns no result.
- [ ] For the same conversation id, the same sequence of Anthropic responses and the same query results, a `query_database` call returns the same text content and the same `_meta` as before this change, apart from the duration values in the agent trace. This holds for both streaming and non-streaming Anthropic requests.
- [ ] An Anthropic API error raised during a call still produces an `isError: true` result, and a database error or statement timeout raised by a runner still produces a failed `run_sql` step that the agent can re-plan from, as before this change.
- [ ] A database query run under a profile whose `max_rows` is lower than the base config's fetches at most that profile's `max_rows` plus one rows from the driver.
- [ ] The change leaves these as they are: - It adds no interruption of work already running on a worker thread. A cancelled call's database query keeps running until it finishes or the engine's statement timeout stops it. Nothing but the query's own end stops it when `statement_timeout_ms = 0`, or when it is a MySQL statement other than `SELECT`, which MySQL's `MAX_EXECUTION_TIME` does not cover. A cancelled call's Anthropic request keeps running, and is billed, until it returns. Server shutdown waits for such threads. - It adds no thread pool of its own. Anthropic calls and database queries share asyncio's default executor, so beyond its thread count further calls wait for a free thread. The ChromaDB memory store keeps its own two-thread pool. - It leaves the synchronous memory-store calls of `import_memory` and the memory-administration MCP tools on the event loop, so those tools still block it while they run. - It leaves the scratch CSV write after each query, `df.to_csv`, and the read-only and row-level-security guards' SQL parsing on the event loop. - It adds no progress notifications and no acknowledge-now / fetch-later job API. A `query_database` call still holds its request open until the agent run ends, so a question that takes longer than a client's timeout still times out for that client.
- [ ] After the change: - `docs/internal/mcp-server/tools.md` states that `query_database`'s Anthropic calls and database queries run on worker threads, that calls sharing a conversation id run one at a time, that a cancelled call's messages are removed from its conversation, and that `import_memory` and the memory-administration tools still block the event loop. - `docs/internal/database-connectors/cleanup-error-handling.md` and `docs/internal/database-connectors/read-only-safety.md` state that a cancelled request's database query keeps running on its worker thread until it finishes or the engine's statement timeout stops it. - `docs/external/getting-started.md` states that a question waiting on the AI service or the database does not stop the server from accepting other requests, and that `import_memory` and the memory-administration tools can still briefly block them.

checklist.claim: The read-only-safety doc asserts that each runner executes its whole `run_sql` body — connect, session set-up, execute, fetch, close — inside one `asyncio.to_thread` call, and that only `statement_timeout_ms = 0` and non-`SELECT` MySQL statements leave nothing but the query's own end to stop it.
checklist.source_excerpt:
Two cases leave nothing but the query's own
end to stop it: `statement_timeout_ms = 0`, which registers no timeout at all;
and a MySQL statement other than a `SELECT`, which `MAX_EXECUTION_TIME` does not
cover.
checklist.verify_against: the three runners' timeout registration code
checklist.verify_hint: Check the `_statement_timeout_ms` branches in `src/sqllens/agent/integrations/{postgres,mysql,sqlite}/sql_runner.py` for any third case (e.g. Postgres connect_timeout, SQLite progress handler granularity)
checklist.evidence: First half verified: postgres/sql_runner.py:127, mysql:94, sqlite:96 each call asyncio.to_thread(self._run_sql_blocking); the bodies cover connect, session setup, execute, fetch, close (mysql 98-172, sqlite 98-148, postgres 130+). Timeout registration: postgres sql_runner.py:150 (>0 only), mysql:111/118 (>0 only; MAX_EXECUTION_TIME is a no-op for non-SELECT per comment 119-122), sqlite:125 (>0 only). So the two named cases are real. The 'only two cases' absolute part is not settled. SQLite's progress handler (sqlite sql_runner.py:127-129) fires only every _PROGRESS_HANDLER_INSTRUCTIONS VM opcodes, so a single long-running opcode or C function would not be interrupted. I did not run this or check the SQLite behavior, so I can't tell whether that is a third case. MySQL read-shaped non-SELECT statements (e.g. SHOW) are covered by the 'other than SELECT' wording. Missing evidence: a SQLite run showing an uninterruptible single-step query, and the is_read_shaped definition.

checklist.evidence: create_conversation (conversation_store.py:52-61) seeds exactly one user Message, and get_conversation returns None for an unknown id (66-72). But the claim also says it returns None for a conversation 'rolled back to empty'. truncate_messages (93-124) only does `del conversation.messages[length:]`; it never removes the conversation from _conversations. get_conversation tests `if conversation and ...`, and Conversation is a pydantic BaseModel (agent/core/storage/models.py:31) with no __bool__/__len__, so it is truthy. A conversation truncated to length 0 is therefore returned with empty messages, not None. The test helper _messages (test_query_database_queue.py:114-117) handles both None and empty, which fits this. tools/query_database.py only calls truncate_messages, never delete_conversation.
